extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London readers interested in manners, courtship, and conduct essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing conduct/society essays and related pastoral and moral narratives: how to depict social tactics (courtship), manage company, craft descriptive pastoral scenes, and argue against scandal and defamation. Includes concrete behavioral 'rules' used as material for essays or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship by apparent disinterest (two-man contrivance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's general conduct should be agreeable, without addressing in particular to the woman he loves; he should seem void of any thoughts as a lover so that a rival's passionate addresses make him appear more desirable by contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Damon and Strephon: one man (Damon) openly languishes and professes passion, the other (Strephon) courts by seeming indifferent and by civil visits immediately after the passionate rival has tired the lady. Tactics include coordinated appearances, contrasting dress and manner, timing visits after the rival's protestations, and using apparent disinterestedness to win a 'sensible' woman who values being desired rather than pitied. Warning: women should examine their feelings before settling a heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and examine your own feelings before disposing your heart
rubrics_metrics.description: In the disposal of your heart, you should know what you are doing, and examine it before it is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice aimed at women: reflect on motives and effects of courtship before committing; if already begun to favor someone won by covert tactics, consider forcing an explicit explanation to test and possibly reset affections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose company of temper suitable to your own
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who has it in his power to choose his own company should, to the best of his judgment, take such as are of a temper most suitable to his own; where that choice is wanting, or one is mistaken and must remain in company, it is in his interest to carry himself as easily as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is practical guidance for social selection and self-management: prefer companions whose dispositions match yours; if stuck with incompatible people, practice ease and patience to avoid creating or escalating discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring a stock of good-humour into country retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When leaving town for country solitude, take with you as great a stock of good-humour as you can, because country life lacks many of the town's reliefs and requires the ability to enjoy leisure and retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country life has fewer amusements (no play-houses, no coffee-house variety), so one must be prepared to spend more time 'within themselves.' The practical upshot for essayists: stress the inward quality (good-humour) needed to make pastoral leisure agreeable; target readers who cannot live without constant company to cultivate the capacity for retirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective rules for preserving ease (the 'Infirmary' system)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal set of rules among a company to preserve ease and tranquillity: a 'wing' of the house acts as an Infirmary where anyone who utters peevish words or shows uneasiness is conveyed until they petition and by manner of submission appear fit for society again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified infractions include ill-natured words, noisy expostulation, speaking impatiently to servants, making someone repeat themselves, showing inattention or 'dishumour'. Procedures: immediate removal to chambers, relief only after an acceptable petition and majority approval. There is a provision that voluntary withdrawal when one senses ill-humour coming is rewarded on return with high marks of esteem. Use as a template for composing satirical or prescriptive pieces about rules and social governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral description via sensory detail and personification of seasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose tranquil garden and seasonal scenes using sensory detail (moonlight, rustling leaves, songs of birds, coolness), classical allusion, and personification of months/seasons as characters with clothing, attributes, movement, and attendant mythic figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example technique: open with a relatable sensory moment (a cool still evening), invoke poetic lines (Milton), then present a dream/vision in which Spring, Mars, Venus, the Months, and attendant deities/processions move in sequence—describe garments, gestures, scents, sounds, and changing temper to convey the year's revolution. Use contrasts (e.g., Mars' armour vs Venus' softness) and progressive decline toward winter to dramatize temporal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautionary anecdote structure for moral lesson (alchemical tale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame a short narrative (anecdote) that reveals a secret or promise (here alchemical revivification/wealth), then show human failing (delay, greed, inattention) leading to ironic misfortune; finish with a moral implication or footnoted source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story elements present: solemn bequest of secret knowledge, explicit procedural constraints (must act within ten hours), character contrasts (pious founder vs dissolute heir), dramatic failure (delay/broken phial), and a concluding moral observation about the vanity of transmitting legacy to unworthy offspring. Useful model for moralizing tales in essays—include dialogue, vivid detail, and a concluding interpretive remark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate gossip and scandal by source credibility (reject hearsay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not credit reports lacking a named origin or supported only by those who themselves 'forgot who told them' or who obtained it from persons of little consideration; such testimonies are too slight to have credit against a person's honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending against scandal, trace back the rumor; identify whether it is grounded or merely circulated by indiscriminate mouths. The oratorical test: if no reliable, named witness or direct source exists, dismiss the accusation. Use this standard in essays arguing against defamation and in depicting social epidemics of rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defamation and the delight in others' misfortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination to defamation is a sign of an ill heart; those who are harmless and innocent have no gratification from speaking ill of others. Little minds prize the number of votes on their side, but true fame follows merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both an ethical and rhetorical axiom for conduct writers: admonish readers against reveling in gossip, emphasize self-examination ('why should virtue provoke?'), and use character sketches (the gossiping old woman Lady Bluemantle) to exemplify the vice. Suggest constructive replacements—benevolence, moderation, and restraint in speech.
